Hertz found that ultraviolet light made a spark pass more readily between metal electrodes. This was an early observation associated with the photoelectric effect.
Lenard showed that light shining on a metal surface releases negatively charged particles—electrons—which can produce a measurable current.
Above the threshold frequency, increasing light intensity increases the number of emitted electrons and hence the photoelectric current, but not their maximum kinetic energy.
The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases with light frequency; below a metal's threshold frequency, emission does not occur regardless of intensity.
